name: fd
workload: Search a home directory (about 750,000 subdirectories and 4 million files, warm disk cache) for the 546 files matching [0-9].jpg; hyperfine means; fd runs with -u so it does the same work as find.
claimed_speedup: fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' 854.8 ms vs find -iregex 19.922 s (README: approximately 23 times faster) and vs find -iname 11.226 s (about 13 times faster).
tradeoffs: Respects .gitignore and skips hidden files by default (the benchmark needs -u to match find's work); regex search by default instead of glob; parallel traversal uses all cores.
caveats: README itself says this is one particular benchmark on one particular machine. CPU model, find version, filesystem and build flags are not stated, so tier A is not met. The speedup mixes multithreading (fd parallelizes traversal, find is single-threaded) with regex-vs-glob matching, so it is not a per-core efficiency win. Benchmark scripts are in sharkdp/fd-benchmarks (opened: README only, scripts not read or run). GNU find was not confirmed to be built at -O3.
found_via: GitHub: README of sharkdp/fd (Rust rewrites of C command-line tools); not in KNOWN_LIST.
why_faster: Parallelized directory traversal (README feature list: 'Very fast due to parallelized directory traversal').

name: sd
baseline: sed (version and implementation not stated; C)
workload: Find-and-replace on files with hyperfine --warmup 3: simple quote replacement over about 1.5 GB of JSON, regex replacement over a 55 MB JSON file, and a 1M-line 36 MB file in line-by-line and across (-A) modes.
claimed_speedup: Simple replace on about 1.5 GB JSON: sd 0.997 s vs sed 2.365 s (README: about 2.35 times faster). Regex replace on a 55 MB JSON file: sd 0.942 s vs sed 11.239 s (README: about 11.93 times faster). On the 1M-line file plain 'foo' to 'qux': sd -A 125.6 ms, sed 316.4 ms, sd default line-by-line 357.0 ms (slower than sed).
tradeoffs: Regex syntax follows what JavaScript and Python users know (README), not sed's; does one job (find and replace) rather than sed's full language; across mode uses 74 MB vs 3 MB for line-by-line on the 36 MB file.
caveats: README calls its comparison examples cherry-picked. Hardware, sed version (GNU or BSD) and build flags are not stated. Default line-by-line mode is slower than sed for a plain literal replacement; the large wins are on regex replacement, where the two tools use different regex engines, so it is an engine and workload comparison rather than a language effect.
found_via: GitHub: README of chmln/sd (Rust rewrites of C command-line tools); not in KNOWN_LIST.

name: hck
workload: Select fields 1,8,19 from a roughly 7 million line CSV (all_train.csv derived files) with a one-character delimiter and with a multi-character or regex delimiter; hyperfine, output to /dev/null.
claimed_speedup: Comma delimiter: hck -Ld, 1.198 s and hck -d, 1.649 s vs GNU cut 7.541 s and awk 4.993 s (README relative column: cut 6.30x and awk 4.17x the fastest hck run; about 4.6x and 3.0x vs plain hck -d, , derived from page data). Space delimiter after tr -s: hck 6.171 s vs cut 7.471 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmarked hck binary; README recommends RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' and a PGO build via just install-native.
hardware: Ubuntu 20, AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16-core), 64 GB DDR4, 1 TB NVMe
tradeoffs: Drop-in-like cut with regex delimiters and header-name selection, but regex delimiters are 5x slower than fixed delimiters; GNU cut has no multi-character delimiter support, so those rows needed a tr -s pipe.
caveats: README says the numbers are not authoritative. It is not stated whether the benchmarked hck was built with target-cpu=native or PGO. The README does not explain the -L flag used in the fastest rows. xsv, tsv-utils and choose are compared too; tsv-select (D) is within 1.4x of the fastest hck row.
found_via: GitHub: README of sstadick/hck (Rust rewrites of C command-line tools); not in KNOWN_LIST.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (tsv-filter, tsv-select, tsv-summarize, tsv-join)
baseline: mawk 1.3.3/1.3.4, GNU awk 4.2.1, GNU cut 8.25/8.29, GNU Datamash 1.3 (all C)
workload: April 2018 study on multi-GB TSV files (4.8 GB/7M lines, 2.7 GB/14M lines, 1.7 GB/86M lines): numeric row filter, regex row filter, column selection, join, summary statistics, CSV-to-TSV; times in seconds.
claimed_speedup: Linux table: numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 s vs mawk 11.31 s vs GNU awk 42.80 s; column selection tsv-select 4.79 s vs mawk 9.51 s vs GNU cut 14.46 s; summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 s vs GNU Datamash 48.51 s. Losses: GNU cut wins narrow column selection (5.60 s vs tsv-select 8.26 s) and xsv (Rust) wins the regex row filter (7.97 s vs 8.80 s).
compiler_and_flags: LDC (LLVM D compiler) release builds; exact flags not in the 2018 report. docs/Performance.md says LTO and PGO builds gave significant gains (details in lto-pgo-study.md, not opened).
hardware: Linux: commodity cloud machine, 16 CPUs, Intel Haswell 2095 MHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04; macOS: Mac mini, 3 GHz Intel i7 (2 cores), 16 GB
tradeoffs: TSV only (no quoting rules), single-threaded tools, D toolchain needed to build; tools are not exact equivalents of awk or cut (limited expression language).
caveats: First-party study from March 2017, updated April 2018 (old tool versions). The report says tools differ in design goals and are not exact equivalents, and that results are I/O dependent. Compared tools include other Rust and Go programs (xsv, csvtk) that sometimes win. Hardware is not a named CPU model, flags are not listed. The wins over C tools come mostly from awk or cut doing more general work.
found_via: GitHub: eBay/tsv-utils README and docs/Performance.md (QUEUE.md and data/wave12/leads.md named it as a wave 14 lead); not in KNOWN_LIST.
why_faster: Per the study text: straightforward D with GC allocation avoided in hot paths, higher-level I/O primitives, and LDC LTO plus PGO builds ('significant performance gains').

name: sort-research-rs (ipnsort, driftsort, Rust std sorts)
baseline: C++ standard library std::sort and std::stable_sort, plus C/C++ sort libraries vendored in the repo (e.g. cpp_pdqsort, c_fluxsort, c_crumsort, cpp_powersort)
workload: Hot benchmark sorting 10k u64 over patterns ascending, descending, random, random_d20, random_p5, random_s95 and random_z1, stable and unstable sorts.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only in text: 'the current Rust standard library unstable sort implementation outperforms the C++ standard library counterparts' (stable and unstable result charts are PNG images, no numeric table in the writeup).
compiler_and_flags: Linux 6.5; rustc 1.75.0-nightly (2023-10-03), --release with lto=thin; clang 16.0.6 and gcc 13.2.1 for native code, build settings in build.rs (not read)
tradeoffs: Generic comparison-based sorts with a strict-weak-ordering contract; ILP and branchless partition rather than SIMD; ipnsort and driftsort contain unsafe code for code-gen; the writeups also analyse UB safety of C, C++ and Rust sorts.
caveats: Numbers exist only as chart images, so the speedup is not quantified in text. The repo author co-wrote ipnsort and driftsort (bias disclosed in the ipnsort writeup). Toolchains are from late 2023 and the writeup warns results are not directly comparable across toolchain updates. Which libstdc++ and libc++ std::sort entries were charted is inferred from the plural 'C++ standard library counterparts' (libc++'s new std::sort is discussed separately as untested). The 'Rust std sort' tested is the 2023 nightly one; the ipnsort and driftsort writeups (2024) mainly compare against Rust std sorts.
found_via: GitHub: Voultapher/sort-research-rs README and writeup/sort_safety; not in KNOWN_LIST.
why_faster: Author: C++ standard library sorts are usually quite old; Rust side uses a branchless partition and sorting-network small-sort for instruction-level parallelism (ipnsort and lomcyc_partition writeups).

name: SPARKNaCl
baseline: TweetNaCl (C), compiled into the same binary with the same GNAT compiler at the same -O level
workload: CPU cycles for one Ed25519 Sign operation on a 256-byte message on a SiFive HiFive1 Revision B (32-bit RISC-V); also Curve25519 and SHA512 analysed.
claimed_speedup: README states the goal 'Performance of the code should be competitive with the C implementation of TweetNaCl'. Cycle counts at -O0/-O1/-O2/-O3 are in AdaCore blog posts and a FOSDEM 2022 abstract that were not reachable here (search snippets only; one snippet said SPARK was close at -O1 and a little behind at -O2 in the 2020 baseline, and the FOSDEM abstract was summarized as outperforming TweetNaCl by about 3x). No numbers on the opened page.
compiler_and_flags: GNAT Community 2020/2021 (CE 2021 is GCC 10.3.1 based; CE 2019 GCC 8.3.1); optimization levels -O0 to -O3 compared; test Makefile has a fast variant with no run-time checking and -O3
hardware: SiFive HiFive1 Revision B (32-bit RISC-V SoC)
tradeoffs: Full SPARK proof of absence of run-time exceptions (needs CVC4 and Z3), TweetNaCl-compatible API, readable constant-time code; results are for a small RISC-V core and do not transfer to x86.
caveats: Evidence snippet-only: blog.adacore.com and archive.fosdem.org are EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the cycle table was not seen. README says the author is still to 'document and explain these results'. Results vary strongly with -O level (loop fusion made -O2 worse in 2021). Not an x86 gcc -O3 comparison. A verifier with blog access should read 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl' and 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)' before keeping a tier.
found_via: GitHub: rod-chapman/SPARKNaCl README; WebSearch snippets of AdaCore blog posts.
why_faster: Per search snippets only ('formal is fast'): the proof of absence of run-time errors lets the code run without run-time checks; README keeps TweetNaCl's constant-time algorithms.

name: verztable
baseline: Abseil, Boost and Ankerl C++ hash tables (README does not name the exact types)
workload: u32, u64 and string keys, sizes 100 to 1M elements, 16 operation mixes (random and sequential insert, reserved insert, update, lookup hit and miss, tombstone, delete, iteration, churn, mixed, read-heavy, write-heavy, zipfian); ns per operation; C++ tables called through FFI.
claimed_speedup: README: 'on average faster than the top C++ hash tables'. BENCHMARKS.md, 100-element u32 set: Reserved Ins. 5 ns vs Abseil 13 / Boost 14 / Ankerl 9; Delete 4 ns vs 13 / 6 / 6; Lookup Miss 1 ns vs 5 / 2 / 3; Tombstone 5 ns vs 16 / 6 / 8. Losses in the same table: Rand. Lookup 3 ns vs Boost 2 ns, Write-Heavy 12 ns vs Ankerl 8 ns.
compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseFast; C++ compiler and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Uses about 25% more memory than the C++ tables (12.0 KB vs 8.0 KB for 1K u32 keys, 12.0 MB vs 8.0 MB at 1M); Zig only.
caveats: Own harness, no CPU model, C++ build flags missing. The 'std' column in the tables is Zig's std hash map (README: 'Abseil, Boost, Ankerl, and Zig's std hash maps'), not std::unordered_map. Boost wins several lookup rows and Ankerl wins write-heavy rows in the table I read, so 'on average faster' rests on the README's aggregate plots (PNG, not readable). FFI to C++ adds overhead to the baseline. Verstable (C) is the algorithmic inspiration, not a benchmark target; the string fast path (strings up to 8 bytes packed in a u64) is not used by the competitors.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/performance?l=zig description 'faster than the top C++ hash tables'; README and BENCHMARKS.md of ThobiasKnudsen/verztable.
why_faster: README: hash-fragment filtering skips non-matches without touching bucket data; fast path for strings of 8 bytes or fewer; stores full 64-bit hashes for string keys to skip memcmp.

hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image
name: Zig (kostya/benchmarks base64)
baseline: Hand-written scalar C base64 (no library), gcc and clang, -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Base64 encode and decode of a 131072-byte string, 8192 tries, into newly allocated buffers; seconds.
claimed_speedup: Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s (about 1.3x and 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Rust 0.842 s is also faster than both. The same table has C/clang with aklomp/base64 at 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7x faster than Zig.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (std.base64); C and C++: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 or clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23 / c++23 -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk)
caveats: No mechanism is given by the source, which caps the tier at C. Zig uses its standard-library base64 while C is a separate hand-written table-driven implementation, so this compares two implementations, and the best C implementation (aklomp SIMD library) is far faster than Zig. The README states no compiler flags in prose; flags were read from common/commands.mk and the base64 Makefile. Values are medians with MAD from one machine.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README tables (cross-language suite named in QUEUE.md section E).
tradeoffs: Single task microbenchmark; Zig std.base64 is scalar.
